description: NASA Space Apps 2026'da Dancing with the SARs için ekip kuruyoruz. Yapay zekâ, fizik ve görüntü işlemeye odaklanıyoruz. Python, veri analizi, uzaktan algılama ve yazılım geliştirmeye ilgi duyan, sorumluluk alabilecek takım arkadaşları arıyoruz.
summary: RSynthesis AI turns forty years of NASA satellite observations into an estimate of the world’s inland surface water, from 1984 to 2030. On an interactive website, it maps how surface water changed across 266 countries using Landsat records, shows seven live NASA and JRC satellite layers for any 12-day NISAR cycle, and links each country’s water to rainfall, temperature and El Niño. For the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar is central: radar sees water through clouds, day or night, where optical sensors cannot. Two transparent statistical engines — a Ridge regression for one-year forecasts and a Bayesian model for probabilistic projections to 2030 — turn the record into estimates with honest uncertainty, validated by leave-one-year-out testing (3.77% mean error across 200 countries). Water is essential and its future is uncertain; our tool gives planners a forward, per-country estimate they can inspect, built entirely on open data.
details:
What it does. RSynthesis AI estimates the world’s inland surface water from the past into the future. It maps how surface water changed across 266 countries and territories from 1984 to 2018 using NASA Landsat records, links each country’s water to its rainfall, temperature and El Niño, and projects surface water to 2030 as probabilities rather than a single guess. Our challenge is “Dancing with the SARs,” so NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar sits at the centre of the project alongside six other NASA and JRC Earth-observation layers.

The website is the product. Everything runs live in the browser at rsynthesisai.earth: a 3D globe of 266 countries where you pick a year and compare two places; seven stacked satellite layers for any 12-day NISAR cycle (NISAR radar, OPERA radar and optical water, VIIRS floods, GPM rainfall, a true-colour photo, and 35 years of Landsat history); a side-by-side “compare” slider that aligns the same place at two moments; a history view showing the rain, heat and El Niño behind every year; an interactive 2030 projection with its uncertainty range; a “what the dry years teach” analysis run on every country; and an AI assistant that answers only from the project’s own data, demonstrated on the Okavango Delta.

Our algorithm is what sets us apart — not just “AI.” Behind the maps are two transparent, tested statistical engines, not a black box. (1) A Ridge regression forecasts next year’s water area in km² from past water and climate, learning the log of the area ratio and clamping the result to between half and twice the last reliable area. (2) A Bayesian engine fits all 32 combinations of five candidate causes — this year’s rain, last year’s rain, a temperature anomaly, El Niño, and a long-term trend — scores each by exact evidence, and model-averages them with a Zellner g-prior, a Scott–Berger prior that penalises over-fitting, and heavy-tailed Student-t errors. It then simulates thousands of possible future years to produce a median, 80% and 95% ranges, and the probability of a below-average or record-low year. We validated it honestly: leave-one-year-out testing over 2013–2018 gives a mean error (WAPE) of 3.77% across 200 countries — edging the naïve “repeat last year” baseline (3.81%) — and every estimate carries its uncertainty. We treat machine learning as one tool; our real contribution is a transparent probabilistic model that quantifies what it does not know.

Benefits and impact. The system turns decades of satellite observation into a forward-looking, per-country water estimate with honest uncertainty, so planners can compare any country, continent or the whole world, see where water was lost, and flag risk years before they arrive — all on open NASA data anyone can inspect.

Tools, languages and data. The web app is built in HTML/CSS/JavaScript with three.js for the 3D globe and map tiles served through NASA GIBS, deployed on Vercel; the Ridge and Bayesian engines run client-side in the browser. A Python data pipeline (using earthaccess for NASA Earthdata/ASF and HDF5 for the NISAR granules) fetches and renders the satellite layers. Data sources: NASA–ISRO NISAR, NASA OPERA, NASA LANCE VIIRS, GPM IMERG and NOAA-20 VIIRS; Landsat (USGS/NASA); EC JRC / Google Global Surface Water; UNEP SDG 6.6.1; Copernicus ERA5; and the NOAA Oceanic Niño Index.

Creativity and factors considered. We put SAR radar to work for water, run a real Bayesian model in the browser so anyone can explore it, and chose to show honest probability ranges instead of a single false-precision number. We were deliberate about the limits and state them openly: we measure surface area only — not depth, volume, groundwater or quality — our causes are associations rather than proof, we cannot know future rainfall, and the country records end in 2018.
